home.story_title: Started by Rädda Barnen. Run by Bangladesh.
home.story_alt: Mothers and babies being seen on the centre's veranda
story: Radda began in 1974 as a project of Rädda Barnen, Swedish Save the Children, to bring mother and child health care to the poorest families of Mirpur. For twenty years Rädda Barnen ran and funded the centre.
In 1994, with the permission of the Ministry of Health, the centre passed into Bangladeshi hands. It has worked alongside the government ever since, under a volunteer Board of Trustees.

list.body: Regular check-ups during pregnancy catch problems early and keep mother and baby safe. We see mothers through pregnancy and in the weeks after birth.
items: Postnatal care for mother and newborn

list.label: Child health
list.title: Vaccines and child health
list.alt: A health worker vaccinating a baby held by its mother
list.body: We give every child the government's Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) schedule, protecting against the main childhood diseases, including the Hepatitis B vaccine for babies under one year. We also offer additional vaccines for children and adults.

list.label: Community health
list.title: Family planning and community health
list.alt: A health worker counselling a mother who holds her child
list.body: Every family has the right to decide when to have children. Our counsellors explain the options in private and help couples choose the method that suits them. Our teams also work in the community, through our static clinics and satellite clinics.

list.label: Support services
list.title: Laboratory tests
list.body: Each of our three permanent clinics has its own laboratory, so most routine tests can be done during your visit, at an affordable cost.

list.label: Training and research
list.title: Training the next generation of health workers
list.body: Through the Radda Paramedic Institute and our training and research work, we prepare health workers to serve mothers and children in communities across Bangladesh.

about.h1: Fifty years beside the mothers of Mirpur
about.lead: Radda was founded to give the poorest families in Mirpur the same quality of care as anyone else. That is still our purpose.
about.pull: A mother and child in Mirpur deserve the same quality of care as anyone, anywhere.
about.lede: Radda MCH-FP Centre is a non-profit health centre in Mirpur, Dhaka. MCH-FP stands for Maternal and Child Health and Family Planning, the work we have done since our first day.
who: We serve families on low incomes, many of whom live in informal settlements, at little or no cost. Our health workers run three permanent clinics with laboratories, satellite clinics in the community, and an immunization programme in partnership with the Government of Bangladesh.
We are governed by a Board of Trustees and funded by the government, partners and individual supporters.

impact.trend_intro: Choose a service to see how it has changed. The report gives 1994, the year the centre passed into Bangladeshi hands, and then each year from 2014.
fund_body: When Rädda Barnen handed the centre over in 1994, it still paid 91 percent of the costs. Its support ended completely in 2004.
Today the centre pays its own way. In 2021-22 its income was Tk 721.90 lakh, with no foreign donation. The money came from what clients pay for services and from joint projects with partners.
impact.partners_intro: Radda works inside the government health system and alongside national and international partners. These are the partnerships named in the 2021-22 report.

gov.name: Dhaka North and Dhaka South City Corporations
gov.role: Routine immunization (EPI) and national immunization days with both city corporations, and the COVID-19 vaccination campaign with Dhaka North.

gov.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
gov.role: The Radda Paramedic Institute runs its two-year Community Paramedic course under the Ministry.

projects.name: Plan International Bangladesh
projects.role: Primary and adolescent health care in five low-income communities of Dhaka South. 1,154 sponsored children received health care in the year.

projects.name: IDKIDS (We Act for Kids)
projects.role: Free primary health care, since 2018, for about 1,000 children at 25 informal schools in Dhaka's slums.

projects.name: Swisscontact (ASTHA project)
projects.role: An e-learning platform for the two-year community paramedic course, piloted at the Radda Paramedic Institute from September 2021.

projects.name: Alive & Thrive
projects.role: Better nutrition counselling for pregnant women, infants and young children in urban clinics.

projects.name: MDF, supported by Nuffic
projects.role: A one-year training programme for Radda's staff, funded by the Dutch government.

projects.name: Mutual Trust Bank
projects.role: Support for 12 students of the Radda Paramedic Institute who could not otherwise afford the course.

impact.thanks: The report also thanks Concern Worldwide, UNICEF, EngenderHealth, RTM International, World Vision Bangladesh, Max Foundation, Compassion International Bangladesh, BAPSA and BRAC for working with the centre.
campaigns_body: Radda takes part in the government's national health campaigns. In 2021-22 its teams gave deworming medicine to 12,450 schoolchildren and reached 12,298 children in the Vitamin A Plus campaign, against a target of 13,066.
The centre also marks the days that keep health in public view, among them World Population Day, World Breastfeeding Week, Global Handwashing Day and Safe Motherhood Day.
institute_body: Radda also trains community health workers. Its institute runs a two-year Community Paramedic course under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, approved by NIPORT. The first batch began in 2011.
In 2021-22 it had 112 students, 76 women and 36 men. They practise at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital and in Radda's own clinics.

rebuild.lead: In the early hours of 25 September 2026 our Mirpur-1 centre was attacked, looted and largely demolished. Vaccination restarted the next day, under a tarpaulin by the road. Rebuilding the rest will take help.

facts.label: The night the Mirpur-1 centre was attacked
One permanent and three semi-permanent buildings demolished
The loss we stated in the case filed with the police
Mothers and children being seen again by 30 October, against about 350 before

what.text: Shortly after midnight on Friday 25 September 2026, a group of 200 to 250 people entered our Mirpur-1 centre. They held two security guards and spent several hours demolishing the centre with heavy machinery. One permanent and three semi-permanent buildings were brought down.

Medical equipment, medicines, vaccines, family planning supplies and government registers were taken, along with an ultrasound machine, a generator, refrigerators and air conditioners. In the case filed with Shah Ali police station we put the loss at more than Tk 1.5 crore.
According to reports on 28 September, police had arrested 11 people and recovered two truckloads of goods.

timeline.title: Vaccination under a tarpaulin
timeline.body: On Saturday, the day after the attack, staff began vaccinating children again under a tarpaulin beside the road.

timeline.title: Into one cleared room
timeline.body: Services moved into a damaged room that had been cleaned out. It had no electricity, water or toilet.

timeline.title: Two rooms in use
timeline.body: The boundary wall has been rebuilt and a new gate fitted. Services run from two rooms. About 250 mothers and children are seen each day, against about 350 before.

missing: There is no working laboratory at the centre; samples are sent elsewhere
Repairs continue in the other rooms
The rooms in use have no fans
